client: I've been really struggling since I got promoted last month. The new responsibilities are weighing on me so much that I lie awake at night worrying I'm not good enough for this role. Part of me thinks I should just be grateful for the opportunity, but the self-doubt is making it hard to focus at work.
therapist: It sounds like you’re carrying a lot of pressure and self-doubt right now, and your tone suggests that this is really weighing on you. Let’s take a moment to unpack these thoughts—what evidence do you have that you’re not good enough for this role, and could there be another way to look at this situation?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I feel like there’s so much evidence that I’m not good enough—like how my manager pointed out mistakes in my last project, and how I always seem to take longer than others to figure things out. It’s hard to see another way to look at it because those things feel like proof that I’m not measuring up. I guess I’m just scared I’ll never be able to meet expectations.
therapist: Your voice carries a lot of worry and frustration, and it’s clear these thoughts about not measuring up are really weighing on you. Let’s explore this further—could it be possible that your manager’s feedback was meant to help you grow rather than as a sign you’re not good enough? And what about the fact that you’re still figuring things out—might that be a normal part of adjusting to a new role?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client:
I get what you're saying about the feedback being meant to help, but it's hard to see it that way when I feel like I'm constantly falling short. Every time I think I've got the hang of things, there's some new criticism that makes me question if I'm cut out for this role at all. 

The "figuring things out" part makes sense logically, but I still can't shake this nagging feeling that everyone else is adjusting faster than I am. Like maybe I'm the only one struggling this much.
therapist: I hear the frustration and urgency in your voice—it sounds like this is really overwhelming for you right now. Let’s pause for a moment and consider whether comparing yourself to others might be adding unnecessary pressure—what if everyone is struggling in their own way, even if it’s not always visible?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, very rapid speech

client: I get what you're saying, but it’s hard not to compare myself when it feels like everyone else has it together. I see people on social media succeeding, happy, and surrounded by friends, and it just makes me feel like I’m failing. Even if they’re struggling too, it doesn’t change how alone I feel right now.
therapist: Your voice sounds tense and rushed, and I can hear how deeply this comparison is affecting you. Social media often shows only highlights, not the behind-the-scenes struggles—could we explore what it would feel like to focus less on others’ journeys and more on your own progress, even if it’s small?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I get what you’re saying, but it’s hard to focus on my own progress when everyone else seems so far ahead. I know it’s not productive, but I can’t help it—it’s like I’m wired to compare myself.
therapist: Your voice sounds a little shaky, and I can hear the frustration and discouragement in your words—it seems like this cycle of comparison is really draining for you. Let’s take a step back and challenge that thought: what if focusing on your own journey, even in small steps, could help you feel less stuck in this cycle of comparison?

client: I get what you're saying about focusing on my own journey, but it's just so hard when I see everyone else seemingly doing better than me. Every time I try to stop comparing, I just end up feeling worse about myself because I can't seem to measure up no matter what I do.
therapist: Your voice sounds soft and strained, and I can hear how much this struggle is weighing on you—it seems like the comparison has become a heavy burden. client: I get what you're saying about focusing on my own growth, but it's hard not to compare myself when I see people my age already buying houses or getting promotions. therapist: Your voice sounds a bit higher than usual, and I can hear the underlying tension and discouragement as you share this—it’s clear that these comparisons are deeply unsettling for you. Let’s explore this further: what if falling behind is more about how you’re measuring success rather than your actual progress? Could there be a way to reframe what “success” means for you, personally?

client: I guess I do feel tense—it’s just hard not to compare myself when everyone around me seems to have it all together. Reframing success sounds nice in theory, but I don’t even know what success would look like for me anymore. Everything feels so out of reach, and I worry that if I lower my standards, I’ll just end up settling for less than I’m capable of.
therapist: You sound really conflicted—on one hand, you want to move past these comparisons, but on the other, you’re worried that redefining success might mean giving up on your potential. That tension comes through in your voice, and it makes sense this feels so unsettling. Let’s slow down—what if “lowering standards” isn’t about settling, but about creating goals that feel meaningful *and* achievable for *you*?

client: I get what you're saying about making goals more achievable, but it still feels like I'd be letting myself down somehow. The idea of setting different standards just makes me feel like I'm making excuses for not being good enough.
therapist: Your voice sounds both rushed and quiet, and I can hear how much this inner conflict is wearing on you—it’s like you’re caught between what you think you "should" do and what actually feels right for you. Let’s explore this: what if "good enough" isn’t about matching others’ milestones, but about honoring your own pace and values? Could that shift the pressure you’re carrying?
